site.name: EcoScienceHub
site.tagline: Peer-informed writing on ecology, biology, and applied physics
site.description: Independent, scientifically literate writing on ecology, biology, and applied physics. Built to be read slowly and cited carefully.

ecology.label: Ecology
ecology.description: Long-form, peer-informed writing on the systems that sustain life — ecosystems and their services, the climate that shapes them, and the biodiversity that gives them resilience.

biology.label: Biology
biology.description: Cellular, molecular, evolutionary, and developmental biology — the mechanisms that connect a single sequence of bases to the diversity of living form.

physics.label: Applied Physics
physics.description: Applied physics for the climate transition and beyond — energy systems, thermodynamic limits, and the quantum foundations that increasingly matter outside the lab.

ecosystems.label: Ecosystems
ecosystems.description: Forests, wetlands, oceans, soils — how energy and matter move through living systems and what disturbance reveals about them.

climate-change.label: Climate Change
climate-change.description: Drivers, feedbacks, attribution, and the policy-relevant uncertainties at the frontier of climate science.

biodiversity.label: Biodiversity
biodiversity.description: Why species count is the wrong metric, what genetic and functional diversity actually do, and where conservation efforts are working.

earth-systems.label: Earth System Science
earth-systems.description: The planet as one coupled system — how the atmosphere, ocean, ice, land, and life exchange energy and matter, and what that coupling explains that no single component can.

earth-observation.label: Earth Observation
earth-observation.description: How satellites and sensors observe the planet — the methods, data products, and uncertainties behind measuring environmental change from space.

cells.label: Cell Biology
cells.description: The cell as the fundamental unit of life — its architecture, energetics, signaling, and the methods used to study it.

genetics.label: Genetics
genetics.description: Molecular genetics, genomics, and the evolution of genetic systems — what sequencing has revealed, what it cannot resolve.

evolution.label: Evolution
evolution.description: Selection, drift, development, and the modern synthesis — including the parts of it that are quietly being revised.

energy.label: Energy
energy.description: Generation, storage, transmission, and the materials and architectures that determine which technologies actually scale.

thermodynamics.label: Thermodynamics
thermodynamics.description: The laws that bound every physical system — and the surprisingly modern questions still open at their frontier.

quantum-basics.label: Quantum Basics
quantum-basics.description: Quantum mechanics for the practitioner — the parts that matter for sensors, materials, and computing, without the philosophy.

conservation.label: Conservation Science
conservation.description: Protected areas, species recovery, restoration, and invasive-species management — what conservation interventions achieve, and how that is measured.

oceans.label: Oceans & Marine Science
oceans.description: Ocean circulation, chemistry, productivity, and marine ecosystems — how the ocean works as a habitat and as a component of the climate system.

freshwater.label: Freshwater & Wetlands
freshwater.description: Rivers, lakes, groundwater, and wetlands — the smallest reservoirs in the water cycle and the most heavily used, and what determines their condition.

forests.label: Forests & Land Cover
forests.description: Forest structure, disturbance, carbon, and land-cover change — what forests do biologically and what they are counted as doing in carbon accounting.

soils.label: Soils & the Land Surface
soils.description: Soil formation, soil carbon, soil biology, and land degradation — the thin, slow-forming layer that most terrestrial life depends on.

pollution.label: Pollution & Environmental Quality
pollution.description: Air, water, and chemical pollution — sources, exposure pathways, measurement, and the evidence linking contaminants to ecological and human harm.

microbiology.label: Microbiology
microbiology.description: Bacteria, archaea, fungi, viruses, and the microbial communities that run most of the planet's biogeochemistry.

physiology.label: Physiology & Organismal Biology
physiology.description: How bodies work — respiration, circulation, thermoregulation, immunity, nervous systems, and development, in humans and other organisms.

taxonomy.label: Taxonomy & the Tree of Life
taxonomy.description: Naming, classifying, and reconstructing relationships among organisms — and the surprisingly unsettled question of how many species there are.

biotechnology.label: Biotechnology & Bioinformatics
biotechnology.description: Sequencing, genome editing, synthetic biology, and the computational methods that turn biological data into inference.

climate-physics.label: Atmospheric & Climate Physics
climate-physics.description: Radiation, atmospheric structure, convection, and the physics that determines how energy moves through the atmosphere and ocean.

mechanics-waves.label: Mechanics, Waves & Fluids
mechanics-waves.description: Motion, forces, energy, oscillation, sound, light, and the behaviour of fluids — the classical physics that underlies most measurement.

matter-radiation.label: Matter, Materials & Radiation
matter-radiation.description: Atomic and nuclear structure, radioactivity, particles, and the materials science behind detectors, reactors, and energy technologies.

home.meta_title: Peer-informed writing on ecology, biology, and applied physics
home.hero_title: Slow, careful writing about the systems that sustain us.
home.hero_lede: EcoScienceHub is a platform for ecology, biology, and applied physics — written by working scientists, edited for clarity, and cited where it matters. Built to be read slowly.
home.mission_title: Science is a slow conversation. We give it the room it needs.
home.mission_p1: Most of what passes for science writing today is optimized for the attention economy. Headlines outrun evidence; nuance is the first thing cut. We started EcoScienceHub because the alternative — careful, cited, accountable writing — is harder to find than it should be.
home.mission_p2: Every article on this platform is organized into a topic hierarchy (Topic → Subtopic → Article), written by a working scientist or experienced science journalist, and kept current with explicit revision dates. When we update something, we say so.

insights.title: Arguments worth defending
insights.description: Insights are short, structured essays. Each one stakes a single, falsifiable claim and defends it. They are written to be argued with — clearly, cited, and dated.
insights.insight_kind_note: This is an argued synthesis of published work by the {desk}, not original research and not a peer-reviewed paper. Its claim is the editorial position; the evidence it rests on is cited below and can be checked independently.

discussions.title: Curated scientific questions
discussions.description: Not a forum. Each entry is a question where the science is genuinely unsettled, framed by an editorial desk with the evidence on each side set out. There is no open commenting.
discussions.about_body: Each question is opened and framed by an EcoScienceHub editorial desk. The notes below the framing are editorial, written by the desk — they are not contributions from named researchers, and no comment on this site is from a member of the public. If verified external contributors take part in future, their entries will be marked and attributed to them by name.
discussions.closed_notice: EcoScienceHub does not accept public submissions on these questions. The notes above are editorial. If you work in one of these fields and want to contribute, write to info@helperg.com — a named contributor would be published under their own name and identified as such.

tools.title: Tools
tools.description: Scientific calculators whose arithmetic is tested and whose constants name the body that recommends them.
tools.count: {count} tools. Every constant comes from a named authority and every calculation is covered by automated tests.
tools.no_js: This calculator needs JavaScript. The formula, the constants and the explanation above do not.
tools.err_counts: Enter counts separated by commas or spaces.

wavelength.name: Wavelength and frequency converter
wavelength.summary: Convert between wavelength and frequency for electromagnetic radiation, and see which region of the spectrum the result falls in.
wavelength.explanation: For an electromagnetic wave the product of wavelength and frequency is the speed of light: c = λf. Because the metre is defined from the speed of light, that relationship in vacuum is exact — a wavelength of one metre corresponds to exactly 299 792 458 hertz, not approximately.
wavelength.assumptions: The default refractive index of 1 is vacuum. In a medium the phase speed is c/n, so a given frequency has a shorter wavelength; enter the medium's refractive index to see that. The spectral region is assigned from the vacuum wavelength.
wavelength.caveats: The boundaries between spectral regions are conventions, not physics. Nothing changes at 400 nm; the eye simply stops responding. Different fields put the ultraviolet–X-ray boundary in different places. This tool also assumes a non-dispersive medium: in a real material the refractive index itself depends on wavelength.

tools.refractive_hint: 1 is vacuum. Air is about 1.0003, water about 1.333.
tools.same_units: Use the same time unit for both.
tools.per_time_unit: Per time unit, as a decimal.
tools.counts_hint: One count per species, separated by commas or spaces. Zeros are species not observed.
tools.any_mass_unit: Any mass unit; the answer is in the same one.
tools.ambiguous_trailing_zeros: Trailing zeros with no decimal point are ambiguous; write the number in scientific notation to be unambiguous.

energy.name: Energy unit converter
energy.summary: Convert between joules, watt-hours, calories, electronvolts and the British thermal unit, with each definition stated.
energy.explanation: Energy has one SI unit and a long list of practical ones, and most of the practical ones are defined exactly in terms of the joule. A watt-hour is exactly 3600 J because the hour is exactly 3600 seconds. A kilowatt-hour is exactly 3.6 MJ. The electronvolt is not a rounded convenience factor at all: it is the elementary charge in coulombs, numerically, and that constant became exact when the SI redefined the ampere in 2019.
energy.assumptions: Every factor here is exact by definition except where the note beside a unit says otherwise. Conversions are performed through the joule, so a round trip returns the original value to the limit of double precision.
energy.caveats: This converts energy, not power. A kilowatt is a rate and a kilowatt-hour is a quantity, and confusing them is the most common error in energy reporting. The tool also says which calorie it means — the thermochemical one, exactly 4.184 J — because there are three in circulation and they differ.

photon.name: Photon energy calculator
photon.summary: The energy of a single photon from its wavelength or its frequency, in joules and electronvolts.
photon.explanation: A photon's energy is Planck's constant times its frequency, E = hf, or equivalently hc/λ. Both h and c are exact by SI definition, so for a stated vacuum wavelength the photon energy is exact too. The electronvolt is the natural unit here because it puts atomic and molecular energies near 1: a visible photon is a few electronvolts, which is why visible light drives chemistry and radio waves do not.
photon.assumptions: Vacuum wavelength. Energies are for one photon, not for a beam — a beam's power is this energy times the number of photons per second.
photon.caveats: This is the energy of a photon, not a dose, not an intensity and not a rate. Whether radiation of a given photon energy can ionise a molecule depends on the molecule as well as the photon, and this tool says nothing about biological effect.

decay.name: Radioactive decay calculator
decay.summary: How much of a radioactive sample remains after a given time, from its half-life.
decay.explanation: Radioactive decay is a random process for any single nucleus and a precisely predictable one for a large number of them. After one half-life, half the original nuclei remain; after two, a quarter; after n, a fraction of one over two to the n. The tool also reports the decay constant λ = ln 2 / t½ and the mean lifetime τ = 1/λ, which is longer than the half-life because the distribution has a long tail.
decay.assumptions: A single decay channel with a constant half-life, and enough nuclei for the statistics to be smooth. Time and half-life must be in the same unit; the tool does not know which one you chose and does not need to.
decay.caveats: This is an educational calculation of a physical quantity. It is not a radiation dose, not an activity in becquerels without knowing the nuclide, and it is not, in any form, guidance for medical, occupational or environmental radiation decisions.

population.name: Population growth models
population.summary: Exponential and logistic growth, side by side, with the assumptions each one makes stated.
population.explanation: Exponential growth assumes a constant per-capita rate: every individual contributes the same increment regardless of how many there already are. Logistic growth adds one thing — a carrying capacity K at which the rate falls to zero — and that single change turns a curve that goes to infinity into one that levels off. Both are two-parameter sketches of something far more complicated.
population.assumptions: A closed population with no immigration or emigration, no age or stage structure, no time lag between crowding and its effect, and a constant environment. The logistic further assumes that the effect of crowding is linear in density.
population.caveats: These are models, not forecasts. A fitted logistic curve is a description of past data, not a prediction of a ceiling, and populations routinely overshoot, cycle, or collapse in ways neither equation contains. Real carrying capacity is not a constant: it depends on the environment, which the population is itself changing.

diversity.name: Diversity index calculator
diversity.summary: Shannon and Simpson diversity from species counts, computed together because either one alone is misleading.
diversity.explanation: Both indices combine how many species there are with how evenly individuals are spread among them, and they weight that combination differently. Shannon, −Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ, is relatively sensitive to rare species. Simpson's D, Σ pᵢ², is the probability that two individuals drawn at random are the same species, and is dominated by the common ones. Two communities can be ranked differently by the two indices — which is a property of the indices, not a contradiction in the data.
diversity.assumptions: The counts are a random sample of the community, and every individual is identified to the same taxonomic level. The indices depend only on the proportions, so multiplying every count by the same factor changes nothing.
diversity.caveats: Neither index says anything about which species are present. A diverse community of weeds and a diverse community of endemics score the same. Both are also sensitive to sampling effort: rarer species appear as the sample grows, so comparing indices computed from samples of different sizes compares the sampling as much as the ecology.

carbon.name: Carbon and carbon dioxide mass converter
carbon.summary: Convert between a mass of carbon and a mass of carbon dioxide, the factor of 3.664 that is most often dropped.
carbon.explanation: A tonne of carbon and a tonne of carbon dioxide are not the same quantity of anything. When carbon burns, each carbon atom picks up two oxygen atoms, and the resulting molecule is heavier than the carbon it came from in the ratio of their molar masses: 44.009 to 12.011, or about 3.664. A budget quoted in gigatonnes of carbon and read as gigatonnes of CO₂ is wrong by nearly a factor of four.
carbon.assumptions: Molar masses come from the CIAAW standard atomic weights, and the ratio is computed from them rather than typed as a constant. The answer is in whatever mass unit you entered.
carbon.caveats: This converts mass, not emissions and not warming. Converting other greenhouse gases to a CO₂-equivalent is a different operation entirely, involving a global warming potential and a chosen time horizon, and it is not what this tool does.

notation.name: Significant figures and scientific notation
notation.summary: How many significant figures a written number carries, and the same number in scientific notation.
notation.explanation: Significant figures are a claim about precision, written into the number itself. Leading zeros never count — they only place the decimal point. Zeros between significant digits always count. Trailing zeros count only when a decimal point is written, which is why 1500 is ambiguous and 1.500 × 10³ is not. Scientific notation exists partly to remove that ambiguity.
notation.assumptions: The ordinary convention above. A number given in scientific notation is read as having exactly the figures written in its mantissa.
notation.caveats: Significant figures are a rough stand-in for uncertainty, not a substitute for it. A measurement reported as 2.50 m does not mean the uncertainty is exactly 0.005 m; it means the person writing it thought two decimal places were justified. Where an uncertainty is actually known, it should be stated.
